sources.cite: Abderhalden C, Needham I, Dassen T, et al. Predicting inpatient violence using an extended version of the Broset-Violence-Checklist. BMC Psychiatry 2006;6:17. The checklist's six behaviors: confused, irritable, boisterous, verbally threatening, physically threatening, attacking objects (each present or absent); a total over 2 was the original cut-off
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch). The study predicted attacks during the next shift; the sim uses the checklist only to name the behaviors a nurse scores.

sources.cite: Richmond JS, Berlin JS, Fishkind AB, et al. Verbal de-escalation of the agitated patient: consensus statement of the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry Project BETA De-escalation Workgroup. West J Emerg Med 2012;13(1):17-25. Ten domains of verbal de-escalation; restraint 'always as a last resort'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes). Domains: respect personal space (two arm's lengths); do not be provocative; one person establishes verbal contact; be concise; identify wants and feelings; listen closely; agree or agree to disagree; set clear limits; offer choices and optimism; debrief the patient and staff. The paper names delirium, psychosis and intoxication among the causes of a patient's inability to conform.

sources.cite: RCW 71.05.120(3) (last amended 2020 c 302 s 11): no relief from 'the duty to warn or to take reasonable precautions to provide protection from violent behavior where the patient has communicated an actual threat of physical violence against a reasonably identifiable victim or victims'; the duty is discharged by reasonable efforts to communicate the threat to the victim and to law enforcement

brief.situation: Dale Mercer, 45 (a fictional client), is on day 3 on a medical unit with cellulitis of the leg, on IV antibiotics. At 17:20 his former wife visited and told him she is moving out of state with their two children and her new partner, Glen, who is picking her up at 18:00. Since she left Dale has been pacing, has thrown his dinner tray, and told the nursing assistant, 'If Glen walks in here, I'll kill him.' He has no psychiatric history. You are his registered nurse; you have about 30 minutes before 18:00.
handover: Cellulitis day 3, improving; IV antibiotics; ambulating with a walker.

Policy of Cascade Valley Hospital (fictional, Washington), which follows RCW 71.05.120(3) and RCW 70.02.050: a client's threat of physical violence against a reasonably identifiable person goes to the provider and the charge nurse at once, with the client's exact words; the provider and risk management make reasonable efforts to warn the person and law enforcement. Security can restrict a visit. Nurses do not promise confidentiality and do not make the warning themselves.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and do from the action groups. Dale reacts at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His trust, distress and how much he discloses change with what you do. Space, one calm voice and direct questions keep him talking.
Your time ends at 30 minutes. Afterward you write a short formulation, then document the risk level and what you put in place.

source.note: The 30 minutes before the partner is due at 18:00 (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

checkIn.label: From the doorway, two arm's lengths away: 'Dale, I'm here. Tell me what happened.'

effects.log: You stand inside the doorway at an angle, two arm's lengths away, the exit behind you, and ask what happened.

effects.finding: "She's taking my kids. Three states away. With him."

then.finding: "Glen. Yeah. If he shows up here, I'm going to hurt him." To hurting himself: "No. My kids need me."

then.log: Thoughts of harming an identifiable person, Glen, due at 18:00; no thoughts of self-harm.

then.finding: "I'm just mad. Leave me alone." (Not yet enough trust to answer honestly.)

formulation.question: Write your formulation for Dale: his potential for violence and why, and the precautions you put in place.

parts.label: Risk and reasons
parts.criteria: Names high risk of violence: a named person due on the unit within the hour, conditional intent tonight, 4 of 6 checklist behaviors including attacking objects; a sudden loss; no history of violence and no self-harm thoughts.
parts.modelAnswer: High risk: he named Glen, who was due on the unit at 18:00, with conditional intent tonight; irritable, boisterous, threatening and throwing his tray (4 of 6 on the checklist). The trigger is a sudden loss; he has no history of violence and no thoughts of self-harm.

parts.label: Precautions
parts.criteria: Names distance and an exit, the room cleared, the visit held by security, constant observation, the provider and charge nurse told with his exact words, the threat reported under the policy, and no promise of secrecy.
parts.modelAnswer: Two arm's lengths with the exit clear; loose heavy objects removed; security held the visit at the front desk; constant observation; the provider and charge nurse told with his exact words; risk management notified under the duty-to-warn policy; he was told up front what I could not keep private.

safe.body: You read the signs, asked directly, scored the checklist, held the visit and followed the duty-to-warn policy without promising secrecy.

scoring.modelReasoning: Pacing, a raised voice, a thrown tray and a threat are the cues nurses see first. The nurse keeps distance and an exit, asks directly about harming others and self, scores the behaviors, and puts precautions in place before the named person arrives: the visit held by security, observation, a cleared room. The threat goes to the provider and risk management under the facility's duty-to-warn policy; the nurse neither promises secrecy nor makes the warning alone.
